summary:
South Chungcheong Province stands under South Korea's national framework. South Korean law does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The criminalising instrument is the Military Criminal Act, article 92-6, which penalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment; the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023, and enforcement has been punitive and targeted, with a 2017 military operation that Amnesty International called a gay witch hunt resulting in criminal charges against 32 personnel and a six-month prison sentence for a gay soldier over consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm concerns Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel treated the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition exists and the surgical precondition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court refused to mandate sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had undergone years of hormone therapy that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender people with minor children may have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register: an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a documented problem in judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state: in November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police protected 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates and that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

South Chungcheong Province has its own student human-rights ordinance, enacted on 10 July 2020, whose Article 15 covers gender identity and sexual orientation. The provincial council passed a repeal bill on 24 April 2024; the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education challenged it before the Supreme Court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of execution on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in effect, and the Office of Education argues that repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties. The Republic of Korea's response of 21 February 2025 to the Joint Communication from UN Special Procedures (ref. OL KOR 3/2024) filed the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education and the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education as stakeholders enforcing authorities in the repeal dispute, recording the Seoul office's parallel 11 July 2024 petition and the Supreme Court's 23 July 2024 suspension.
tangentialFactors:
The repeal litigation is not confined to South Chungcheong. South Korea's student human-rights ordinance framework has been adopted by a number of provinces and metropolitan authorities, and Wikipedia's article on the Ordinance of Student Rights lists Chungcheongnam-do among them while recording that its ordinance was revoked in 2024, matching the 24 April 2024 provincial-council repeal vote. The prohibition on student discrimination by gender, religion, nationality, disability, race and sexual orientation runs through the framework, and the provisions on gender and sexual diversity are named as the most contentious items, which explains why repeal efforts cluster on those clauses rather than on the ordinances as a whole.

Two education authorities are litigating in parallel. The Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education filed its own petition against its council's abolition on 11 July 2024 and obtained a Supreme Court suspension on 23 July 2024, three weeks after the Chungcheongnam-do suspension, and both were filed as enforcing authorities in the same UN Special Procedures communication, ref. OL KOR 3/2024.

The national pattern is one of contested, uneven protection. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records a relatively positive overall record on free media and civil society in South Korea alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people, and there is still no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity at national level, which leaves provincial instruments such as the student ordinance carrying weight they would otherwise not bear.
localsOnly:
The student human-rights ordinance in force in South Chungcheong Province was enacted on 10 July 2020. Article 15 prohibits discrimination of students on grounds including gender identity and sexual orientation, and it continues to apply notwithstanding the provincial council's repeal vote of 24 April 2024, because the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education obtained suspension of execution from the Supreme Court on 30 May 2024 after filing suit on 13 May 2024. The Office of Education's position, carried in the Republic of Korea's 21 February 2025 response to UN Special Procedures, is that the repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties.

Discrimination burden measured among residents is high. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, that 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, that 65.4% of those recommended it reported harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the previous year.

The nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health covered 585 transgender and non-binary young adults and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care, mapping stigmatisation against life stages.

Legal gender recognition procedure changed on 8 May 2024, when a court held for five plaintiffs that sex-reassignment surgery cannot be mandated to change legal sex status, and on 24 November 2022, when the Supreme Court allowed recognition for transgender people with minor children provided they are not married.
outOfScopeNotes:
The final Supreme Court judgment on the Chungcheongnam-do repeal bill was still pending as of the Republic of Korea's response of 21 February 2025; the sources record only the interim suspension of execution of 30 May 2024, not a merits ruling, so the ordinance's ultimate fate is unresolved on this inventory.

Which other provinces repealed or retained their student human-rights ordinances after 2024 is not sourced here; the inventory confirms only that South Chungcheong adopted the framework on 10 July 2020 and that its ordinance was revoked in 2024 by council vote, subject to the suspension above.

Whether Military Criminal Act article 92-6 has been enforced against personnel stationed within South Chungcheong Province is not sourced. The inventory records national enforcement in 2017 and the 2023 Constitutional Court upholding, with no provincial case.

Enforcement outcomes for the Seoul Central District Court restroom ruling of 2 July 2024, beyond the 300,000 won symbolic compensation, are not detailed, and no comparable provincial litigation in South Chungcheong appears in the inventory.

Implementation of the National Human Rights Commission of Korea's November 2023 hospitalisation finding is unresolved: the sources record the Ministry of Health and Welfare's refusal to draft guidelines but no subsequent policy.
